intro: To use Word for insurance claims adjusters on Mac well, start with one claim report template saved as a .dotx file, then build every report from heading styles. Those two habits save the most time on each file. Lazur, the voice assistant for the Mac, can point to menu items, guide you one click at a time, and dictate notes at the cursor. Keep claimant data in mind before you hold its shortcut.
tldr: Save one finished claim report as a Word template with File > Save as Template, then save each claim as a new .docx file.
Use heading styles for every section. Bold text does not feed the navigation pane or a table of contents.
Check your build under Word > About Word. Microsoft describes a reduced-functionality mode for Mac that it dates to July 13, 2026.
Hold fn to dictate at the cursor. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask Lazur where a command lives.
Lazur looks at your screen only while you hold its shortcut, so check your carrier's data rules before you hold it over a claim file.

blocks.text: What a claims adjuster does in Word

Word is where the claim report lives. The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes adjusters as people who investigate, evaluate and settle claims. They decide whether the policy covers the loss, set the payment amount, check for fraud and authorize payments. They also gather photographs and statements, then put together a report for claims examiners to review.

The occupation is large. BLS counted 376,100 claims adjusters, examiners, and investigators in employment in 2025. For the combined occupation, which adds auto damage appraisers, BLS projects a decline of 6%, or about 21,800 jobs, from 2025 to 2035. Most of the roughly 21,600 openings each year come from workers who leave the field.

The headcount matters less than your own week. Whatever the numbers do, your report still has to be clear and on time. Word is already open on your desk, so the fastest gains come from how you set it up.
Where to start with Word for insurance claims adjusters on Mac

Start with the report, not the settings. Many of the repeat tasks in a claim file come from rebuilding the same headings and boilerplate for every file. A template fixes that once. Each new claim then starts from a clean page with the structure already in place.

Use this order for a new setup. Build one complete example report with every section. Save it as a template. Replace the sample details with placeholders such as [Claim number] and [Date of loss]. Last, add heading styles and a short checklist at the top.
Set up one claim report template on Mac

Open the finished sample report, then choose File > Save as Template. Type a name, such as Claim Report Template. Pick a location if Word asks for one. Set File Format to Microsoft Word template (.dotx). If the file has macros, choose Macro-Enabled template (.dotm) instead. Click Save.

items: Clean the sample report so it holds placeholders, not real claim details.
Choose File > Save as Template.
Type a name and pick a location if Word asks.
Set File Format to Microsoft Word template (.dotx), or Macro-Enabled template (.dotm) if the file has macros.
Click Save. By default, Word stores templates in the Templates folder in User Content under Group Containers.

blocks.title: Strip the sample data first
blocks.text: A template keeps everything in the file, including sample names, dates, photos and comments. Remove those before you save. A leftover phone number in the template ends up in every new claim you start from it.

Save each claim as a new .docx file, named with the claim number and the date. Never type a live claim into the master template. That keeps the template clean for the next file and keeps each claim separate.
Use heading styles so every report reads the same

Headings do two jobs. They make the report easy to scan, and they give Word a structure it can use. Apply heading styles from the Styles gallery instead of making a line bold and bigger by hand. The navigation pane and a table of contents both read the styles. Manual bold is invisible to them.
The table below is one layout to start from. Change it to match the sections your carrier requires. Keep the same order in every file, so an examiner always knows where to look.

rows: Claim number, insured, date of loss, one-paragraph outcome
What happened, where, when, and who was present
Policy wording you relied on, with section numbers
One subsection per area, each with photo references
Who gave the statement, the date, and a short summary
Amount, basis, and any holdback or deductible
blocks.caption: Suggested heading structure for a claim report

blocks.text: Keep heading levels steady. A Heading 2 should sit under a Heading 1. If a subsection jumps to Heading 3 with no Heading 2 above it, the outline breaks and the navigation view looks wrong.
For the exact steps on Mac, read [how to apply heading styles in Word on Mac](/how-to/apply-heading-styles-in-word).
Review a draft with Track Changes and comments

A reviewer may mark up a draft before it goes final. Track Changes records each insertion and deletion, so the author can accept or reject it. Comments let a reviewer ask a question beside a sentence without changing the text.

Microsoft's published Track Changes steps cover Word on iPad and iPhone. They describe turning on Track Changes from the Review tab, and adding a comment from a long-press menu. The Mac layout can differ, so confirm the exact menu names on your copy of Word before you walk a team through it.
Turn on Track Changes before anyone edits a shared draft. Edits made before you turn it on look like part of the original text, and nobody can see what changed.

blocks.title: Clean up before you send
blocks.text: Accept or reject all changes, then turn Track Changes off. A file full of old revision marks confuses the next reader and can show comments you meant to remove.

For comments in more detail, read [how to add a comment in Word on Mac](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-word). To check two versions side by side, read [how to compare two documents in Word on Mac](/how-to/compare-two-documents-in-word).
Add photos and statements without breaking the layout

A single large photo can push a heading to the wrong page. A caption can drift away from its picture. Put each group of photos in a table, one photo per cell, with the caption under it. The table holds its shape when the text around it changes.

Name every photo with a number and the area it shows, such as P-01 kitchen ceiling. Then refer to it in the coverage analysis as (P-01). Your examiner can match a sentence to a picture without a long search.

Statements need the same care. Write the speaker, the date and the method, such as a phone call or an in-person interview. Put exact words in quotation marks. Paraphrase everything else, and say that you did.
Check your Word version before a filing deadline

Word for Mac updates often, and the version you run can matter when a file will not save. Microsoft's release notes list the latest build as Version 16.114.3 (Build 26102720), dated October 27, 2026. The two builds before it, 16.114.2 and 16.114.1, arrived on October 26 and October 22, 2026.
The Word entries in those three builds say only 'Quality and performance improvements.' They do not name a fix for claim files. To check your own build, open Word and choose Word > About Word.

Microsoft's known-issues page describes a reduced-functionality mode for Mac. In that mode, Word can open and print files but cannot edit, save or create new files. Microsoft says subscribers on macOS, iPhone and iPad might notice this starting July 13, 2026.
Check that page before a deadline. This guide found no later confirmation that the change took effect, so verify it on your own copy. Your license type and build decide what applies to you.

blocks.title: If Word will not save
blocks.text: If Word opens a claim file but refuses to save your edits, stop typing. Write down the changes you made, then check Microsoft's known-issues page and ask your IT team before you continue.
Save, export and lock the finished report
Save with ⌘ S as you go. Save again before every call, meeting or handoff. A manual save takes a second, and a crash can wipe out a long session.

A PDF locks the layout, so the examiner sees the same pages you saw. Export the PDF after your last change, and name it with the claim number and date. Our guide shows [how to save as a PDF in Word on Mac](/how-to/save-as-a-pdf-in-word).

If the report holds personal or medical details, protect it with a password before you send it. The [password guide for Word on Mac](/how-to/password-protect-a-document-in-word) covers the steps. Send the password in a separate message, through a channel your carrier allows.
Recover a report that disappeared

Crashes happen, and so do closed windows. Before you rewrite a lost section, check the recent files list and look for an autosaved copy. The [guide to recovering an unsaved document in Word on Mac](/how-to/recover-an-unsaved-document-in-word) walks through the checks in order.
Keep the master template and your open claim files in a folder that backs up. A lost copy is much easier to replace when a second copy already exists.
Mistakes that slow adjusters down in Word

items: Typing the claim number into every section by hand. One typo then appears in several places. Enter it once, then copy it from there.
Bolding headings instead of applying heading styles. The navigation pane and table of contents miss them.
Saving a live claim over the master template. Save a new .docx file first.
Pasting full-size photos. Large images make the file slow to open and slow to send. Resize them before you insert them.
Leaving Track Changes on in a final file. The next reader sees every old edit.
Dictating into the wrong window. Click into the right paragraph, then hold fn.

blocks.text: Use Lazur for the steps you keep looking up

Lazur lives in the notch on your Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask a question about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Lazur runs on macOS only. It is not a plugin or add-in for Word or any other app.

items: Point: Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control on your screen.
Guide: Lazur walks you through each step and waits for each click.
Explain: Lazur explains a dialog or an error message in plain words.
Dictate and draft: Lazur types text at the cursor, or drafts text for you to edit.

blocks.text: Lazur does not click buttons, edit your file or operate other apps for you. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time. You do the clicking, and it waits for each one.
Protect claimant data while you work
Claim files hold names, addresses, bank details and sometimes medical information. Before you put any of that on screen, check your carrier's data rules. This page does not replace those rules.

Here is how Lazur handles what is on your screen. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
Close files you do not need before you hold the shortcut. Dictate claimant details only into the window you intend, and check the cursor first.

blocks.title: Know what you are sharing
blocks.text: Holding the shortcut sends what is on screen to AI providers so Lazur can answer. Do not hold it over a file your company does not allow in an outside tool.
How much time report writing takes

A vendor that sells adjuster AI software says adjusters spend 50% to 60% of working hours on reports, evidence formatting and compliance checks. The same article says a typical property or motor report takes 3 to 5 hours to write by hand. It adds that each rejected report costs 1 to 2 hours of rework.

The article names no study or data source for those figures. Treat them as a rough signal, not a benchmark. The useful move is to measure your own reports for one week. Note how long each report takes, and how often a reviewer sends one back.

blocks.title: Where the figures come from
blocks.text: The numbers come from FieldScribe AI, a company that sells software to adjusters. The article cites no study for them.
A workflow for one claim, from first draft to final

items: Open the template and save it as a new .docx file named for the claim.
Write the claim summary first, in one short paragraph.
Hold fn and dictate the loss facts as you read your notes.
Write the coverage analysis with the policy wording open beside it. Quote section numbers exactly.
Turn on Track Changes if a reviewer will mark up the draft.
Accept or reject the changes, turn Track Changes off, and save.
Export a PDF, name it, and send it through your usual system.

blocks.text: Each step is small. Together they stop one claim from turning into three versions in three folders.
What to do next

Start with the template this week. Once it exists, every later claim begins faster. Add one habit at a time, such as heading styles one week and dictation the next. faq.question: Does this guide need a special edition of Word for Mac?
faq.answer: No special edition is needed for the template steps here. They follow Microsoft's standard Mac steps for saving a template. Check Word > About Word to see your build, and keep Word updated.

faq.question: Can I use one Word template for every claim type?
faq.answer: You can, but a separate template for each claim type is easier to manage. If auto and property claims need different sections, save one .dotx file for each. Keep the names clear.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my Word file for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at controls, guides you one click at a time, explains messages, answers out loud, and types or drafts text when you ask.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.

faq.question: Is claimant data safe to use with Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your carrier's rules still apply, so check them first.

faq.question: Why does Word say a file is in reduced functionality mode?
faq.answer: Microsoft's known-issues page describes a reduced-functionality mode for Mac. In that mode, Word can open and print files but cannot edit, save or create them. The page dates this to July 13, 2026. Check that page and your IT team before a deadline.

faq.question: Are the Track Changes steps the same on Mac as on iPad?
faq.answer: Microsoft's published Track Changes steps cover iPad and iPhone. The turn-on step is in the Review tab on those devices. Confirm the exact menu names on your Mac, because the layout can differ.

faq.question: Can I dictate into Word with Lazur?
faq.answer: Yes. Hold fn and speak. Lazur dictates clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, including Word. Check the cursor position before you start.

faq.question: Where do I get Lazur?
faq.answer: Download it from the download page. It starts with a short free trial, and you do not need a credit card to begin. Check the pricing page for current plans.
